name: Dionysius of Alexandria
knownFor: Bishop of Alexandria and pupil of Origen, whose letters Eusebius of Caesarea kept. He urged Novatian not to split the church, wrote against the followers of Sabellius and was defended by Athanasius when the Arians claimed him, and argued from its Greek that the Revelation was written by a John other than the apostle.
dates: Bishop from the third year of the emperor Philip, about 247 in Arthur McGiffert's reckoning; died in the twelfth year of Gallienus, about 264 or 265, after seventeen years as bishop. Around 250, the year of Decius's edicts, is approximate
role: Head of the catechetical school at Alexandria, then its bishop

keyWorks.title: Letters
keyWorks.about: on his flight under Decius, the plague, the lapsed, rebaptism and Novatian, kept in Eusebius's Church History, Books 6 and 7

keyWorks.title: On Promises
keyWorks.about: two books against Nepos, with his study of who wrote the Revelation of John

keyWorks.title: Refutation and Defence
keyWorks.about: four books to Dionysius, bishop of Rome, answering the charge that he called the Son a creature

traces: At Arsinoe, after three days of argument, Coracion, the leader of those who held Nepos's teaching, said he would no longer hold or teach it, Dionysius reports.
He told Stephen, bishop of Rome, that the churches of the East, once divided, were united and at peace. Eusebius says they had rejected Novatian's new teaching.

He wrote on the schism to Fabius of Antioch, who leaned toward it, to Cornelius of Rome, and to the Roman confessors who held with Novatian, and again after they came back to the church, Eusebius says.
remembered: Eusebius calls him the great bishop of the Alexandrians.
Athanasius of Alexandria wrote a defense of him a century later, when the Arians claimed him, on the grounds that he had explained himself and died honored in the church.

Basil of Caesarea, in a letter, judged that in his zeal against Sabellius he went too far the other way, like a woodman who pulls a sapling crooked on the other side, and that, as far as Basil knew, he first gave men the seeds of the Anomoean teaching. In another letter Basil calls him the great Dionysius.

uncertain: His own account. The flight under Decius, the peace of the eastern churches and Coracion's change of mind are all known from Dionysius's own letters, kept by Eusebius.

The charge of flight. Eusebius says only that Germanus, a bishop of his time, tried to slander him; that the charge was flight is read from Dionysius's answer, that he did not flee on his own impulse. Arthur McGiffert, who translated Eusebius, says Germanus accused him of cowardice and that his see is not known.

His years. No ancient source used here gives a year in our reckoning. Eusebius dates his election to the third year of Philip and his death to the twelfth year of Gallienus; McGiffert reckons these as 246 or 247 and 264 or 265, and dates Decius's edicts to early 250.
Those with him in the flight. McGiffert says the word Dionysius used is read as children, pupils or servants.
The words to Novatian. His Greek says that Novatian ought to have suffered anything at all rather than split the church. The old English "it were better" softens a rebuke into advice.

The dispute with Dionysius of Rome. Athanasius defends him: he explained himself, showed himself of right opinion and died honored in the church. Basil judges that he went too far against Sabellius. Archibald Robertson, an editor of Athanasius, says his four books put an end to the controversy. Blomfield Jackson, who translated Basil, notes that B. F. Westcott quotes Lumper as putting Basil's charge down to imperfect knowledge of his writings.

Rebaptism. Eusebius keeps letters in which he pleads with Stephen of Rome for the churches that rebaptized heretics, says he received from Heraclas the rule of taking such converts back without another baptism, will not overturn the synods of Iconium and Synnada that did rebaptize, and asks Xystus of Rome for counsel about a man baptized among heretics. Jerome says he agreed with Cyprian and the African synod on rebaptism. Basil wonders that he accepted the baptism of the Pepuzeni. No source used here gives Stephen's or Xystus's answer.

The Revelation. He judged from its thought, words and Greek, beside the Gospel and letter of John, that the apostle did not write it, though he would not reject the book. Before him, he says, some had rejected it altogether. Eusebius, in an earlier book of his History, thinks it probable that the second John saw the Revelation, unless one will admit the first, and lists it among the accepted books and among the rejected, if it seems proper. No ancient source says Dionysius moved him; McGiffert thinks Eusebius was thinking of Dionysius's argument.

quotationOriginals.modern: It would have been right to suffer anything at all rather than split the Church of God.
quotationOriginals.printed: For it were better to suffer everything, rather than divide the Church of God.
quotationOriginals.work: Dionysius, letter to Novatian, in Eusebius, Church History VI.45, tr. Arthur McGiffert
quotationOriginals.uncertain: Our English follows the Greek (Schwartz, lines 7363-7364, with Rufinus's Latin at 7434-7435). The Greek says Novatian ought to have suffered anything at all rather than split the church; McGiffert's "it were better" softens a rebuke into advice. The second reading, "For we ought to suffer anything at all, rather than split the church of God", makes it a general rule; both readings say suffering anything is better than splitting the church.
